blocks.body:
Three houses each need a connection to three utilities: water, gas and electricity. Can all nine pipes be laid in a flat field without any two crossing? People who try it on paper always get stuck with one crossing left. This page explains why it is impossible, and the reason is a simple counting formula that Euler found for polyhedra in 1750.

In graph language (see [[graph-basics]]) the puzzle asks whether the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ can be drawn without crossings. Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$ answers this, and also shows that planar graphs have few edges, can be coloured with few colours, and allow only five regular polyhedra.

blocks.title: Planar graph and faces
blocks.body:
A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane so that edges meet only at shared endpoints. Such a drawing is a plane graph. Removing the drawing from the plane leaves several connected regions, called faces; exactly one of them, the outer face, is unbounded.

Planarity is a property of the graph, while faces belong to a particular drawing. For example $K_4$, drawn as a square with both diagonals, has a crossing, but redrawn as a triangle with one vertex in the middle joined to the three corners it has none, so $K_4$ is planar.

blocks.title: Counting vertices, edges and faces
blocks.body:
Try a few drawings and record $V$, $E$ and $F$ (count the outer face).

- A triangle: $V = 3$, $E = 3$, $F = 2$ (inside and outside).
- $K_4$ drawn as a triangle with a centre vertex: $V = 4$, $E = 6$, $F = 4$.
- The cube, drawn as a small square inside a large one with corners joined: $V = 8$, $E = 12$, $F = 6$.
- A path with $5$ vertices: $V = 5$, $E = 4$, $F = 1$.

In every case $V - E + F = 2$. In particular, redrawing a graph changes the shapes of the faces but not their number, since $F = 2 - V + E$.

blocks.title: Euler's formula
blocks.body:
For every connected plane graph with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces,
$$V - E + F = 2.$$
The formula also holds when the graph has loops or multiple edges.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use induction on the number of edges, keeping $V$ fixed.

If the graph has no cycle, it is a connected graph without cycles, that is, a tree, so $E = V - 1$. A tree drawn in the plane does not enclose any region, so $F = 1$, and $V - E + F = V - (V - 1) + 1 = 2$.

If the graph has a cycle, choose an edge $e$ on it. Removing $e$ keeps the graph connected, because the rest of the cycle still joins the ends of $e$. The cycle is a closed curve without self-crossings, and by the Jordan curve theorem it separates the plane into an inside and an outside. The edge $e$ lies on the cycle, so the face on one side of $e$ is inside the cycle and the face on the other side is outside: these are two different faces. Deleting $e$ merges them into one face and leaves the other faces alone. So the new graph has $E - 1$ edges and $F - 1$ faces, and by the induction hypothesis $V - (E - 1) + (F - 1) = 2$. This is the same number as $V - E + F$.

blocks.title: Planar graphs have few edges
blocks.body:
Walk around the boundary of a face and count the edges you pass; this is the degree of the face (an edge with the same face on both sides is counted twice). Every edge has two sides, each bordering a face, so
$$\sum_{\text{faces } f}\deg f = 2E.$$
This is the face version of the handshake lemma $\sum_v \deg v = 2E$. In a simple graph (no loops, no multiple edges) with at least $3$ vertices, every face has degree at least $3$: a face of degree $1$ or $2$ would need a loop or a double edge, or the whole graph would be a single edge. Combining this with Euler's formula gives a strong bound.

blocks.title: Edge bound for planar graphs
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a simple planar graph with $V \ge 3$ vertices and $E$ edges. Then $E \le 3V - 6$. If in addition $G$ has no triangle (cycle of length $3$), then $E \le 2V - 4$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Adding edges only makes the inequalities harder to satisfy, so we may add edges, keeping the drawing crossing-free and the graph simple, until $G$ is connected: if there were two components, an edge could join a vertex of one to a vertex of the other through a face they both border. (For the triangle-free version, connecting two components this way creates no triangle.) So assume $G$ is connected, and draw it.

Every face has degree at least $3$, so $3F \le \sum \deg f = 2E$, i.e. $F \le \frac{2E}{3}$. Euler's formula gives $2 = V - E + F \le V - E + \frac{2E}{3}$, hence $E \le 3V - 6$.

If there are no triangles, every face has degree at least $4$: degrees $1$ and $2$ are excluded as before, and a closed boundary walk of length $3$ in a simple graph is a triangle. Then $4F \le 2E$, and $2 \le V - E + \frac E2$ gives $E \le 2V - 4$.

blocks.title: Example 1: the utilities and the five towns
blocks.body: Show that $K_5$ (five vertices, all pairs joined) and $K_{3,3}$ (the utilities graph) are not planar.
blocks.solution:
$K_5$ has $V = 5$ and $E = \binom52 = 10$. A planar graph with $5$ vertices has at most $3\cdot5 - 6 = 9$ edges, so $K_5$ is not planar.

$K_{3,3}$ has $V = 6$ and $E = 9$, which is within $3V - 6 = 12$, so the first bound is not enough. But $K_{3,3}$ has no triangles: every edge joins a house to a utility, so any cycle alternates between the two sides and has even length. The triangle-free bound allows at most $2\cdot 6 - 4 = 8$ edges, and $9 > 8$. So $K_{3,3}$ is not planar, and the utilities puzzle has no solution.

Both graphs are only just non-planar: removing any one edge from $K_5$ or from $K_{3,3}$ leaves a planar graph.

blocks.title: Kuratowski's theorem
blocks.body:
If $G$ is planar, so is every subgraph of $G$. Subdividing edges (putting new vertices of degree $2$ in their middle) does not change planarity either way, since a subdivided edge is still drawn as one curve. So a graph containing a subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ cannot be planar. In 1930 Kuratowski proved the converse.

Kuratowski's theorem: a graph is planar if and only if it contains no subgraph that is a subdivision of $K_5$ or of $K_{3,3}$.

Wagner gave an equivalent form: a graph is planar if and only if neither $K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ can be obtained from it by deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges (that is, neither is a minor). Both theorems are stated here without proof; the proofs are considerably longer. The Petersen graph, $10$ vertices of degree $3$ with no cycle shorter than $5$, is a famous non-planar graph that contains no $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ directly as a subgraph, yet contains a subdivision of $K_{3,3}$.

blocks.title: Colouring planar graphs
blocks.body:
Since $\sum_v \deg v = 2E \le 6V - 12 < 6V$, the average degree of a simple planar graph is less than $6$. Hence every simple planar graph has a vertex of degree at most $5$. This one fact drives the colouring theorems (see [[graph-coloring]]).

Six colours always suffice. Use induction on $V$: remove a vertex $v$ of degree at most $5$, colour the rest with six colours, and give $v$ a colour not used by its at most five neighbours.

Five colours also suffice (Heawood, 1890). Proceed as before. If the neighbours of $v$ use at most four colours, a fifth is free. Otherwise $v$ has five neighbours $v_1, \dots, v_5$ in clockwise order, coloured $1, \dots, 5$. Look at the vertices coloured $1$ or $3$. If no path in this two-coloured part joins $v_1$ to $v_3$, swap colours $1$ and $3$ in the part containing $v_1$; now $v_1$ has colour $3$, the colouring is still proper, and colour $1$ is free for $v$. If such a path exists, it forms together with $v$ a cycle that separates $v_2$ from $v_4$ (Jordan curve theorem again), so no path coloured $2$ and $4$ can join $v_2$ to $v_4$; swap colours $2$ and $4$ in the part containing $v_2$, which frees colour $2$ for $v$. These swaps along two-coloured paths are called Kempe chains.

Four colours suffice too. This is the four colour theorem, proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 with a large computer check of unavoidable configurations. It was simplified by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas in 1997 and formally verified by Gonthier in 2005, but no proof without a computer is known. Colouring a map is colouring its dual graph: a vertex per country, an edge per shared border.

blocks.title: Example 2: the five Platonic solids
blocks.body: A regular polyhedron has faces that are all regular $p$-gons, with $q$ faces meeting at every vertex, where $p, q \ge 3$. Use Euler's formula to show there are only five possibilities.

blocks.title: Example 3: twelve pentagons
blocks.body: A football is stitched from pentagons and hexagons, with exactly three patches meeting at every corner. Prove that there must be exactly twelve pentagons, however many hexagons there are.
blocks.solution:
Let there be $P$ pentagons and $H$ hexagons, so $F = P + H$. Counting edges by faces, each edge is shared by two patches: $E = \frac{5P + 6H}{2}$. Counting vertices, each corner is shared by three patches: $V = \frac{5P + 6H}{3}$. The seams form a connected graph on the sphere, which becomes a plane graph after removing a point inside one patch (that patch becomes the outer face), so Euler's formula applies:
$$\frac{5P + 6H}{3} - \frac{5P + 6H}{2} + P + H = 2.$$
The left side equals $-\frac{5P + 6H}{6} + P + H = \frac{P}{6}$. So $P = 12$, and $H$ cancelled out completely. The standard football has $H = 20$ (so $V = 60$, $E = 90$, $F = 32$); the same count explains why fullerene molecules such as $\mathrm{C}_{60}$ always have exactly twelve pentagonal rings.

blocks.title: Example 4: regions cut out by lines
blocks.body: Draw $n \ge 1$ lines in the plane, no two parallel and no three through one point. Use Euler's formula to find the number of regions they create.
blocks.solution:
Make the picture into a finite plane graph. Draw a large circle containing all the crossing points, and keep only what is inside it. The vertices are the $\binom n2$ crossing points and the $2n$ points where lines meet the circle: $V = \binom n2 + 2n$. Each line meets the other $n - 1$ lines, so its chord inside the circle is cut into $n$ edges, giving $n^2$ edges from lines; the circle itself is cut into $2n$ arcs. So $E = n^2 + 2n$. The graph is connected (multiple edges can occur when $n = 1$, which Euler's formula allows).

Euler's formula gives $F = 2 - V + E = 2 - \binom n2 - 2n + n^2 + 2n = 2 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. One of these faces is the outside of the circle, and every other face is exactly one region of the line arrangement, cut off by the circle (unbounded regions reach the circle). So the number of regions is
$$1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.$$
For $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$ this gives $2, 4, 7, 11$. The same answer follows by induction: the $n$-th line crosses $n - 1$ others, so it passes through $n$ old regions and splits each in two.

blocks.body:
- $V - E + F = 2$ needs the graph to be connected. With $c$ components the correct formula is $V - E + F = 1 + c$.
- $E \le 3V - 6$ is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one: $K_{3,3}$ satisfies it but is not planar. Use $E \le 2V - 4$ for triangle-free graphs, or Kuratowski's theorem.
- The outer face counts. Forgetting it gives $V - E + F = 1$, which is the formula for the bounded faces only.
- On other surfaces the formula changes: graphs drawn on a torus so that every face is a disc satisfy $V - E + F = 0$, and $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ can both be drawn on a torus without crossings.

The number $V - E + F$ is the Euler characteristic, an invariant of the surface rather than of the drawing: it is $2$ for the sphere, $0$ for the torus and $2 - 2g$ for a surface with $g$ holes, which is the starting point of [[classification-of-surfaces]] and of [[homology]]. For smooth surfaces it reappears in [[gauss-bonnet]], where total curvature equals $2\pi$ times the Euler characteristic. The colouring results belong to [[graph-coloring]], and the edge bounds are a simple case of [[extremal-graphs]]. The Jordan curve theorem used in the proofs is a basic result about [[topological-spaces|the topology of the plane]]. Planarity testing is a classic topic in [[graph-algorithms]].

1. A connected plane graph has $10$ vertices, each of degree $3$. How many faces does it have?
2. Use the fact that the Petersen graph has no cycles of length $3$ or $4$ to show that it is not planar. (Hint: every face would have degree at least $5$.)
3. Show that every simple planar graph with $V \ge 3$ vertices in which every face is a triangle has exactly $3V - 6$ edges, and check this for the octahedron.
4. Show that a simple planar graph with fewer than $12$ vertices has a vertex of degree at most $4$.
